blocks.text: ومنه لنسفعن بالناصية سفع الطاير لطم اي لنجرنه بها الي النار بجناحية وفلان فلانا او لنسودن وجهه او لنعلمنه لطمه وضربه والشي اعلمه علامة اهل النار والسوافع ووسمه والسموم وجهه لفحه لوايح السموم لفحا يسيرا وبناصيته قبض عليها فاجتذ بها [wa-minhu la-nasfaʿan bi-l-nāṣiya safaʿa al-ṭāyir laṭama ay la-najurrannahu bihā ilī al-nār bi-janāḥiyya wa-fulān fulānan aw la-nusawwidanna wajhahu aw la-nuʿlimannahu laṭamahu wa-ḍarabahu wa-l-shī aʿlamahu ʿalāmat ahl al-nār wa-l-sawāfiʿ wa-wasamahu wa-l-samūm wajhahu lafaḥahu lawāyiḥ al-samūm lafḥan yasīran wa-bi-nāṣiyatihi qabaḍa ʿalayhā fa-ijtadha bihā] The verb سفع [safaʿa], said of a bird, means: it clapped its wings; it also means: it struck with a sound; [III, 185] and likewise, said of one person and another: he struck him with a resounding blow. Also: he branded something with a mark. A pestilential wind is also said to clap or strike someone's face when it scorches him with its heat by a mere breath or touch. Also, with "by the forelock," it means to seize and drag, as in that passage of the Qur'an (Sura 96:15): truly We shall slap their faces by the forelock, that is, We shall seize them by the forelocks and drag them to the fire of Gehenna; or, We shall blacken their face; or, We shall brand them with the mark of the damned in the fire. Finally, those winds are called "clappers" (which strike with a hiss) that scorch and blacken with a pestilential blast. So Firuzabadi, cited by Schultens on Proverb. XXIII, 30., p. 305.

Bochart could have added that the root صقع [ṣaqaʿa] is also preserved in the Arabic dialect, and has the same meaning as سقع [saqaʿa], namely to blow upon, to strike with a blast or with a hiss. Thus Amr ibn Kulthum, in the Mu'allaqa, describing triple-meshed coats of mail: كان غضونهن متون عدر تصفعها الرياح اذا جرينا [ka-anna ghuḍūnahunna mutūnu ʿudrin taṣfaʿuhā al-riyāḥu idhā jarayna] As if their folds were the surfaces of pools which the winds ruffle with their blast, when we are spurred on [III, 186] in our course. So Schultens, loc. cit. It is clear that the two roots, سفع [safaʿa] and صفع [ṣafaʿa], agree with each other not only in sound but also in meaning, since the primary sense of each, to strike, to smite, is transferred first to the scorching wind called Samum, when it touches or strikes someone's face with its heat, and then to any scorching and harmful blast, such as is ascribed to basilisks, which received from this the name צפע among the Hebrews. — Michaelis, in Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. 6, p. 2130, thinks the basilisk seems to have received the name צפע from صُوفَعَة [ṣūfaʿa] a turban: "namely," he says, "it bore something on its head, which some called horns, and so the Greeks named it κεράτην [keratēn]; others compared it to a crown or diadem and called it regulus, βασιλισκον [basiliskon], recognizing it as, so to speak, the king and most powerful of serpents."
